page: Google Cloud Platform n4d-highcpu-80 is an x86_64 architecture compute instance featuring 80 dedicated virtual CPUs and 160 GB of system memory. Engineered for compute-focused requirements within the general infrastructure family, the instance maintains a consistent 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, which provides 2.0 GB of system memory per vCPU.

Hardware provisioning does not include local NVMe or ephemeral SSD storage, requiring all persistent storage and root filesystem mounts to be hosted on network-attached block volumes. The instance includes 0 discrete GPU accelerators and allocates no complimentary public IPv4 addresses, requiring standard cloud networking mechanisms for external connectivity.

By delivering a high concentration of dedicated execution threads without excess memory overhead, the n4d-highcpu-80 configuration exhibits high resource efficiency for tasks bounded by CPU availability rather than memory capacity. The server type is well aligned for distributed continuous integration runners, parallel software compilation, batch processing, video transcode operations, and multi-threaded analytical compute engines.
description: Google Cloud Platform n4d-highcpu-80 is an x86_64 architecture virtual machine provisioned with 80 dedicated virtual CPU cores and 160 GB of system memory. Structured with a 1:2 compute-to-RAM ratio that delivers 2.0 GB of memory per core, the configuration prioritizes high thread counts over deep memory allocations. The instance includes no attached GPU coprocessors and contains no bundled local solid-state storage, directing all filesystem and storage operations across network-attached persistent storage services. Public IPv4 connectivity requires user-provisioned network resources, as complimentary addresses are omitted. The dense vCPU architecture offers qualitative resource efficiency for parallel execution models that do not demand extensive RAM pools or hardware acceleration. This machine type serves compute-heavy tasks including parallel software builds, batch computation pipelines, continuous integration workloads, and data compression workflows.
